messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm doing some N-mixture Poisson modeling of bird abundance point-count data. I know these models are for discrete count data.

However, I have multiple sites with different numbers of point-count stations, so to compare abundance across sites, I have to divide the number of birds detected by the number of point-count stations.
So, for Site Y, Species X abundance ends up being # of Species X/point-count station, which yields a fraction. For example, Species X = 1.57 birds at Site Y.

Here's my question: Does modeling fractions for abundance (pseudo-continuous data) mess up N-mixture Poisson modeling?
This could also be an issue with Chi-square GOF tests, which I think for these models should be for discrete data only too (Bolker 2007).
I've been messing with models in R unmarked package and Royle Biometrics in PRESENCE.

Thanks to anyone who may have a thought on this.

Regards,

Matt B.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Matt,

the Nmix model assumes discrete counts, so your basic data structure must be station by occasion, and the elements in that matrix must be your discrete counts.

If you want to compare "sites", where sites comprise multiple stations, you can treat sites as a factor (= categorical explanatory variable) and use likelihood ratio tests or AIC to find out whether sites differ in expected abundance lambda. You can also predict lambda for the levels of the site factor, to obtain an estimate of the mean expected abundance at each site.

Kind regards  --  Marc

Hi all,

 First off, thanks to those who post answers on this forum, and an especially big thanks to those who developed Unmarked and consistently answer questions from beginners such as myself.

 I am struggling to fit a somewhat complex dataset using pcountOpen (107 sites; 14 primary periods [years, unevenly spaced]; 15-20 secondary periods [depending on closure assumptions for each of several species]; apparently low detectability; many site, yearly, and observation covariates).  I am interested in the effects of timber harvests on population growth or decline for multiple species over time.  The models seemed to be converging with the default dynamics settings, but once I started using dynamics = “trend” I started getting a lot more ‘Hessian is singular,’ ‘Hessian is not invertible,’ etc. messages, as well as runtimes on the order of hours for null models and >20hrs for models with covariates.  Following this, I started wondering if I could just use constant dynamics and derive population trends from changes in survival and recruitment over time.

 I ran the simulated example from the manual, and found that the trend and constant dynamics resulted in different estimates of initial abundance and detection probability.  Moreover, I found that while the dynamics=constant models seemed insensitive to K, the trend models seemed sensitive to K, both in model fit and parameter estimates (this echoes my preliminary work with my data, though for my data the trend models that did run had lower AIC values than constant models). messages.body_plain:
Hi, everyone,
I am a student new to the occupancy model, and have two problems puzzling me for a long time.

1. I surveyed  30 sites in the summer of 2012. In the summer of 2013, I also surveyed 30 sites, but only 10 of them were the sites I surveyed in 2012. That meant, among the 50 sites, only 10 sites had two years' data. Therefore, I have two choices now.
Choice 1: Use single-season occupancy model to analyse each year's data separately, but the cost is lack of sufficient sample size (only 30 sites for occupancy analysis).
Choice 2: Combine two years' data together. For the 10 sites which are surveyed in both years, use the data from 2012 and 2013 as two independent sample. For example, if SiteA is surveyed in both years, make sample "SiteA_2012" and "SiteA_2013" to represent the data from 2012 summer and 2013 summer, and use them in the same way as "SiteB" and "SiteC". But the disadvantage is "SiteA_2012" and "SiteA_2013" are in fact the data from the same location, thus may violate the hypothesis of sample independence.
Therefore, which choice is the better one? Or are there any other solutions?

2. I have measured 13 environmental variables for each site (there is no colinearity between any of them), but as the sample size is so small, I have to reduce the variables. I am reluctant to use PCA because the resulting component is difficult to interpret; but every variable may be meaningful to the result and I don't want to delete any of them. Do I have any other choice?

Thank you very much for any advices ! Best regards,
Sun, Ge

I would recommend doing the 2nd thing , treating the 2 years as independent sites or, as we say in previous postings to the email list "stack the years" (create a bigger data set with years as sites).
There will be very little dependence induced by having repeated measures on only 10 sites.

In a way this is kind of a model-based PCA. You're letting the data find the best linear combination of variables for explaining occupancy.

I'm afraid I have to disagree with Andy's suggestion (2). What Andy propose's isn't really much of an approximation to a PCA, and could get you into trouble.

I've done a lot of PCA analyses over the years (back when 'body size' and 'growth rate' were things I spent a *lot* of time working on. ). PCA offers a lot of advantages:

1\ the principal components analysis is a variable reduction procedure. This is exactly what you want -- and is especially useful when there is a lot of variable redundancy. Further, the components themselves are orthogonal, and tend to have nice statistical properties.

2\  I think the idea that principal components are 'hard to interpret' is frequently a red herring. A PC is simply a  linear combination of optimally-weighted observed variables. It is a linear model  - component terms are interpreted in much the same fashion as beta coefficients in a linear model of the usual sort.

3\ while you can derive PC's for a multivariate dataset pretty easily using a variety of statistical software, there are often a fair number of options, and nuances, you need to work through (standardize variables, or not, rotations, etc). However, for a basis to understand the factors loadings in the components, I usually recommend doing a derivation of the coefficients by hand (at least partially). if you have any background in linear algebra, this is pretty straightforward: deriving the coefficients involves spectral decomposition of the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the variance-covariance matrix for your multivariate data.

 I don't think they should match, in general, when you modify some other component of the model.

 I also think K = 20 is generally too low and it is not surprising to see sensitivity to K when it is set so low. Keep K = 100 or more and then evaluate sensitivity by trying some models with K = 150.

Thanks for everyone here,
I would like to make some supplements:) This is also a problem puzzling me for a long time. I had asked some field scientists who using occupancy analysis, somebody suggest me to pool the daily camera-trap data until the detection probability exceeded 0.1, the others recommended me to pool the data until the mean autocorrelation coefficient of the generated dataset reached the lowest level.
Then I used nine simulated datasets (with different degree of autocorrelation, psi and p) to test their suggestions, and found:
1. The difference of the AIC between best fitted model and true model didn't correlated with dataset's mean autocorrelation coefficient, neither did the detection probability.
2. When the autocorrelation is low, the best fitted model was very similar to the true model no matter how to pool the data;
3. When the autocorrelation is high, the AIC difference between best fitted model and true model is also high no matter how to pool the data, and there wasn't any significant trend or pattern between that AIC difference and mean autocorrelation or detection probability.
Thus my conclusion was, when the daily camera-trap data's modeling result was good, the pooling data's result was also good; when the daily data's modeling result was poor, just pooling the data couldn't generate better results.
However, my simulation was very simple and didn't incorporate replications. Thus I wonder is there any progress abou this issue? How about Rebert's bear data modeling results, please? I am using R-N model to reanalyse my camera-trap data in the hope that it can do better than the previously-used single-season occu model.
Best wishes and thanks a lot for all of the folks here,
Sun, Ge

> Hi folks,

> I'm also really pleased to see this being discussed. For years I've wondered about the ramifications of collapsing camera data arbitrarily for occupancy estimation, especially with fairly sparse carnivore datasets. After discussing this with many statisticians and researchers my take is that--within reason--the results you get should be the same regardless of encounter interval length as long as you 1) interpret estimates using the correct interval length (e.g., 1-day probability of detection if daily encounter histories, 1-week if collapsed over a week), 2) don't create histories that are too sparse or dense (i.e., all 1s), and model any obvious heterogeneity in detection probability (e.g., if you were analyzing using a 1-day interval but baiting a site every two weeks).
>
> I currently have a student looking at this with a black bear dataset--trying various interval lengths for encounter histories and seeing what kind of estimates he gets for p and psi.
>
> Best,
>
> Robert

> On Tuesday, January 20, 2015 at 1:59:11 PM UTC-8, Mathias Tobler wrote:
> > I think the issue has been summarized really well so far but I would like to add a few things based on my experience with camera trap data and occupancy models. While correlation can be an issue on a short time scale (1-2 days) overdispersion of the data is often a bigger issue, especially for abundant species and species with small home ranges. Camera traps are often run over long periods of time (e.g. 60 to 90 days) so that you can potentially end up with a large number of detections. For some species in our dataset the number of days a species was detected at a camera can range from 1 to 35 out of 60 sampling days. This heterogeneity among cameras can lead to a poor model fit. Generally we found that the Royle-Nichols model improves fit but even then there is too much overdispersion when using one day as a sampling period. Pooling the data over 5 or 6 days helps bringing those large numbers down while little affecting the low numbers. So loosing information can be helpful. So far I had little success with modeling the overdispersion using a negative binomial or a Poisson log-normal model. Using a Poisson detection model instead of a Binomial as suggested by Marc did not affect model fit either.
> >
> > Overdispersion is less of an issue for carnivores with large home ranges. Those species cover large areas and spend little time near a single camera. Ungulates or smaller mammals on the other hand can can pass by a camera almost daily in some cases. Some of the differences among cameras can be addressed by covariates such as on/off trail or habitat type but we found that a lot of the variation can not be explained. It is easy to imagine that if a camera is close to an individuals home range center we would get more detections while if the camera is at the edge of a home range we get fewer detections, which is exactly what the SECR models assume. Cameras can also unintentionally be placed close to an important food source, denn, travel path etc. which increases the number of detections compared to other cameras. These detections are not necessarily correlated in time.
> >
> > So my suggestion would be to try to model  your data with a Royle-Nichols model with 1 day as a sampling occasion and the assess model fit. If the model does not fit then I would pool data over several days.
> >
> > Regards,

> > > > > if you discretize and analyse using a standard occupancy model, then you typically lose information, whenever more than a single detection per occasion gets subsumed into a single '1' in the resulting history. Viewed from this angle, it would be best to discretize finely so that you never have more than a single detection per occasion. On the other hand, this may lead to very large data sets (lots of occasions) and moreover, there may be serial dependence, i.e., neighbouring occasions may not be independent samples from the underlying presence/absence process. This is a problem that you would have to deal with by adoping more complex occupancy models, see Hines et al. (tigers on trails paper, 2010) and recent follow-up paper for dynamic occupancy. These models have been implemented in PRESENCE (not sure about MARK). Note that independence or lack thereof in space (as for transect-based sampling) is very similar or identical to that in time (as for your camera-trap data).
> > > > >
> > > > > Some would argue that discretisation of measurements made on a continuous process is always a bad idea and that you should directly model a continuous detection process, in space or in time. This typically leads to Poisson process models, which in the context of occupancy estimation have been introduced by Gurutzeta Guillera Arroita (GGA) (papers in JABES, MEE and elsewhere). The simplest such models assumes independence in space or time. The individual detections can be aggregated into a detection frequency per transect or per camera and some total time interval, say C_i for the number of detections at trap or transect i.
> > > > >
> > > > > Then, you can specify the following variant of occupancy model, which has a Poisson instead of a Binomial description of the observation process:
> > > > >
> > > > > z_i ~ Bernoulli(psi)              # Presence/absence (z) is like a coin flip
> > > > > C_i ~ Poisson(z_i * lambda_i) # lambda is detection rate, i.e., the expected number of detections given that a site is occupied.
> > > > >
> > > > > You can model pattern in occupancy probability by logit(psi_i) = some linear model and those in the detection frequency by log(lambda_i) = some linear model, exactly as in a GLM (this model is the combination of a logistic regression for occupancy and a Poisson regression for the number of detections).
> > > > >
> > > > > This model can easily be fitted in BUGS. Note that for this model, a single replicate is enough (there is no j). Also note that one would usually have an offset in the Poisson part of the model, to account for unequal length (of time or transect) of observation.
> > > > >
> > > > > If you can assume independence, then this seems to be a very useful model. If you don't have independence (for instance, some aggregation of detection in time or space), then this autocorrelation ought to be modelled and you must model the individual detections. One conceptually simple way of doing so is by imagining two latent processes underlying the measured detections, between which there are switches with some probability. GGA have lately developed such a 2MMPP model (a 2-state Markov-modulated point process model --- try to say this a couple of times quickly ....). She has code in Matlab, but I think not (yet) for any language that is widely spoken in ecology, such as R or BUGS.

Do I saturate or minimize the number of cameras?

B

hi Brent,
 I guess I'll  say something about this.
 The interpretation of occupancy models is somewhat imprecise as a result of the practical reality that animals are using some 2-dimensional region and camera traps sample some vague region of space (see this paper by Efford and Dawson 2012 "Occupancy in Continuous Habitat" and also the Chandler and Royle (2013) paper in Annals of Appl. Statistcs for context).

That said I think it's clear that at a large spatial scale (large areal sample units, or cameras spread far apart) the models are telling you something about species distribution (indeed, this is the customary view of every species distribution model) whereas at a small scale occupancy models are telling you something about resource usage (also a customary view, using telemetry equipment).  If you saturate one or a few home ranges of individuals with cameras then you'd be answering the same question that you could answer with telemetry equipment except that you can make direct inferences about probability of use, not just the relative intensity of use. Some would argue that it is not a stretch to go from one to the other, but I guess this is a matter of some debate in the literature.

regards,
andy

Hi, andy and Brent,
The occupancy consistence assumption in microhabitat occupancy analysis is also a long-term problem for me. One key assumption made when conducting the occupancy analysis is that the occupancy state at a site remains constant throughout the season. But in microhabitat analysis of the large mammal habitat selection, this assumption is hard to meet. For my research, I have conducted a camera-trap survey for the roe deer and wild boar. I measured the forestry variables within 60m of each camera-trap and used them as the variables of a single-season occupancy analysis. I initially analyzed the camera-trap photos on a daily basis, i.e. the dependent variable of the occupancy analysis was the presence-absence of the target species within every day's photos. But now I learn that the daily occupancy state of both ungulate species can't be constant within the 60m radius of each camera-site (as theese species's homa-range is far bigger than a 60m radius circle), which violates the basal assumption of occupancy analysis.
I don't know whether it will make the results unacceptable. Now I am thinking about one solution: pool the camera photos so that each sampling occasion is 6-days or 7-days, because within 6-days there must be at least one deer passed through the surrounding area of camera-site ? Is it reasonable or totally wrong?
Thanks for any suggestions! Best regards,
Sun, Ge

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brent,

30 cameras per square kilometer is pretty intensive sampling!  Andy nailed the analytical/inferential trade-offs, but if you could provide a little more detail about your sampling situation, it might become easier to provide feedback.  How large are the treatment polygons with respect to the home range size of your focal species?  Do you have to maintain the stated density at the fixed sampling points throughout the entire 3 month period, or allowed to shuffle cameras around? At what camera density could you maintain systematic coverage of the system (allowing for moving cameras every month, say)?

I guess I'd submit 3 points:
if PAO is your currency for treatment effect, sampling more individuals (wider spacing) is generally likely to be of greater interest than sampling a few individuals with paparazzi-like intensity, but it really depends on the spatial scale of the treatments: if only a few animals are even in a position to use the treatment blocks, than it makes sense to focus on those few animals. If you can't maintain station independence for particular species, then you are better off using a framework that uses correlated observations to estimate something useful rather than try to model away the noise using a spatial random effect or something.
Along those lines, I'd try to select a spacing scale that could estimate density (following the framework of the paper Andy previously mentioned) and individual-space use of species with larger home ranges (treating observations as spatially correlated) and estimate occurrence or abundance of smaller species (treating observations as independent).  In other words, for the species that might only ever exist at a density of 1 or 2 per treatment polygon, treat this as a within home range resource selection question, and for the species that exist at higher densities or use fractional amounts of space, treat it as a population response question.
If your colleague's sampling points inhibit your ability to accomplish the above, perhaps complain politely.  Is your colleague either baiting his/her sampling points or sampling along trails?  I don't expect that a camera hung on a random tree in the woods is likely to be all that productive...

Just my 2 cents.

Thanks for the additional info.  So it sounds like 200 meter spacing, something in that neighborhood, maybe a total sampled area of about 5 square kilometers or so, and maybe 240 camera locations?

messages.body_plain:
Hello to everyone. I was wondering if I could tap in the forums collective knowledge for some guidance on how to tackle potential population closure violation in the analysis of jaguar occurrence data that I collected (and I am currently analysing for my graduate project) using interviews.

I conducted multiple interviews about the presence of jaguars and main prey species within ~130 36-sq.km <http://36-sq.km> cells. During the interviews, I asked the interviewees if they had observed the target species in the field over the previous 12 months. I am concerned that the length of time considered would be violating a) the population closure assumption, esp. for the jaguar since some individuals could be transient through the area and therefore result in detections in multiple cells within my study area.

Is there a way that you suggest I test for population closure? I was reading earlier posts in the forum, and one suggestion by Marc Kerry (for a different type of model, but still relevant) was to run a dynamic (multi-season) model and see if the extinction/colonization parameters suggested closure (i.e. near zero values). My problem is that I have a potentially long study period (12 months) but not accurate information as to when the last detection the interviewees reported was made (some times it is available, but there is enough inconsistency in whether they reported all detections within past years vs. only the last one) to not be comfortable in developing a multi-season detection history. Currently, my survey periods are individuals – not months of the year (e.g. Jan-March, April-June etc.).

I would appreciate very much any advice as to how best to address this potential population closure violation.

Kind regards,
Patricia Calderon

Dear Luciana,

I think that by "backtransform my models" you mean getting predictions of lambda or p, right ? That is, the values of mean abundance and detection that one would expect for chosen values of your covariates, given your model ?

In that case you must use the predict function. As always in R, you first define a new data frame that contains the values for the covariates at which you want to predict lambda or p. Then you call the predict function and supply this new data frame. Here is a template (note also how you must specify factors):

# Two new data sets for prediction: for lambda and for p (200 data points each)

lamNewData <- data.frame(elev = (seq(200, 2250,,200) - mean(tits[,"elev"]))/  sd(tits[,"elev"]), forest = 0, iLength = 1/5.1)

pNewData <- data.frame(elev = 0, time = factor("2", levels = c("1", "2", "3")), dur = 0, date = (seq(1,90,,200) - mean(date, na.rm = T))/sd(date, na.rm = T))

In the new data frames you must specify a value of all covariates that appear in the abundance or the detection part of the model. Note that in my example, I had standardised all covariates (with the exception of iLength), so that a value of 0 corresponds to the average of those covariates.

Once you have that you do something like:

# Predictions for lambda and p, with SE and CIs

predict(fm5, type="state", newdata=lamNewData)    # predictions for expected abundance (lambda)

predict(fm5, type="det", newdata=pNewData)        # same for detection probability

Kind regards  -- Marc
